steps.title: A waiting move gives White a plan

narration.say: Capablanca has White against Kreymborg in 1910. Black chooses a waiting policy instead of active counterplay.
White lifts the rook to d4, restraining f4 and preparing b3. Black moves the rook to f6.
White opens the queenside and brings the king forward.
The rook moves to a1. Black centralises the king, but overlooks the growing pressure on the queenside.
White invades a6. Black defends with the rook.
White doubles rooks on the a-file. Black finally starts counterplay with g5.
White does not immediately collect the a-pawn. First, challenge the kingside pawn advance.

steps.title: Keep the king safe and active

narration.say: White retreats the king, then recaptures on f3 after the pawn exchange.
White plays Ke2. Capablanca criticises this move, preferring an immediate queenside advance.
White pushes h5. Capablanca also criticises this choice; Black then misses a defensive chance by answering h6.
White advances f4. Black shifts the rook, and the white king approaches the centre.
White reaches d4 with the king. Black invades g2, and White rearranges the rooks.
The king retreats to d3. One pair of rooks is exchanged.
The remaining white rook keeps moving while Black defends.
White checks, exchanges on c5, and wins the a-pawn.
Black resigns. The rook activity and central pawns have decided the ending.
A passive waiting policy allowed White to identify targets and double rooks against them.
The game also contains inaccuracies. A coherent plan helps, but every concrete position still needs calculation.
